# Synthesis Principles {.unnumbered}

Parts I through VI built an agentic system one piece at a time and tested each piece on its own terms. The Model priced a single proposal and bounded what search can buy. Agent Memory closed the state exposure, Tool Use closed the authority exposure, and The Agent Runtime closed the horizon exposure, then measured whether the whole single-agent system works. Learning from Trajectories changed the model without moving any exposure, and Agents at Scale multiplied all three across agents and a fleet. Part VII adds no exposure and builds no new closure. It runs every part together on one production trajectory and asks two questions that no single part could answer, which subsystem owns each transition when all of them act at once, and what work remains that none of them can take over.

The first question returns to principles the reader already holds, from invariant closure (principle \ref{pri-invariant-closure}) through the fleet principles of Part VI. Running them together shows that the failures surviving a well-built system live at the seams between parts, where one principle's guarantee meets another's assumption, and that each seam needs a named owner. The second question has a single answer, and it is the volume's final principle.

::: {#pri-vol3-specification-boundary .callout-principle title="The specification boundary"}

**Invariant**: An agent can generate the realization of a design, such as code and configuration, but it cannot author the task contract that governs its own work, meaning the goal, the environment, the permitted actions, the available observations, and the completion criteria. If the accidental work of expressing a design is a fraction $f_{\text{acc}}$ of the engineering effort, accelerating that work without limit bounds the net speedup at $1/(1-f_{\text{acc}})$. The full treatment appears in @sec-vol3-conclusion-brooks.

**Implication**: Engineering effort shifts toward specifying invariants, building the verifiers that accept work, and owning the decision to accept. Faster generation raises the value of that work rather than removing it.

:::

The principle marks where the machine this book built ends. It can close horizon, state, and authority for a task it has been given, and it can check its own work against a predicate that someone has written. Writing that predicate and answering for the result stay with the engineer. @Sec-vol3-conclusion traces one incident trajectory through every part and names the owner and record of each transition. It then turns the task contract into an enforced operating envelope, assigns owners to the seams, applies the intervention ladder and a safety case to decide what to change and when to release, and states the open problems before ending on this boundary.
